omissions_note: This captures every entry in the accessible catalogue, including all 27 S6–S8 spotlights and 594 poster-only entries absent from the recording index. It does not establish that the snapshot is the final official proceedings: Google Sites embeds were not readable, OpenReview’s venue page returned Loading, and a tested individual record requested browser verification. Workshop papers are separate records in coverage.json. Catalogue-reproduced abstracts are available in full; their reported results have not been independently assessed.
matching_note: Talk links are conservative title/name matches; unmatched or uncertain identities are not assigned a video timestamp.

papers.title: FAR: Failure-Aware Retry for Test-Time Recovery and Continual Policy Improvement
papers.summary: FAR addresses the case in which an existing diffusion policy fails and a naive retry repeats the same behavior. It uses critic estimates to select potentially failure-inducing action chunks, pairs them with higher-valued alternatives, and performs a short preference-based policy update before retrying. Smoothed action perturbations provide local exploration. A separate improvement loop combines expert data, successful online trajectories and failed trajectories: the critic learns from the collected experience, while the actor learns from expert and successful data. The reported evaluation covers nine simulated manipulation tasks and three real xArm tasks, with bounded retry budgets. The paper supports distinguishing immediate recovery from longer-term policy improvement, but its autonomy claim needs care: real experiments use a human’s binary success/failure signal, and the arm is returned to its initial configuration between retries while the scene remains changed. Tests use single-task diffusion policies trained from scratch; transfer to large pretrained VLAs and principled automatic failure detection are stated future work.

papers.title: Scale Up Strategically: Learning Compositional Generalization via Bias-Aware Evaluation and Data Collection for Robotic Manipulation
papers.summary: This study asks how a fixed demonstration budget should be distributed across instruction factors, rather than treating data scale as a single count. It deliberately correlates pairs of factors during fine-tuning, then evaluates held-out combinations to diagnose which factor a policy follows when cues conflict. A vision-language judge supplies factor-level failure labels. The authors use those diagnostics to collect more informative combinations under matched demonstration and configuration-change budgets. Their simulation and real-robot studies report benefits from this targeted allocation, but the appendix also identifies settings where the advantage disappears, particularly difficult size distinctions. The contribution is a concrete data-selection perspective: first identify an under-grounded capability, then test whether reallocating examples helps it. The reported hierarchy and improvements are scoped to the tested policies, task factors and collection protocols.

papers.title: ContactGuard: Pre-Contact Execution Monitoring with Action-Conditioned Latent World Models
papers.summary: ContactGuard is an execution monitor for a policy that proposes action chunks. It learns action-conditioned visual dynamics from unlabeled robot trajectories, freezes that latent world model, and trains a small failure probe on labeled pre-contact clips. Before a predicted gripper closure, the monitor rolls the model forward under the policy’s own planned actions and scores the future latent. A task-calibrated threshold can veto the chunk while the underlying policy remains unchanged. The experiments use four grasp settings on a dual-arm robot and compare future-latent monitoring against matched current-state and action-corruption controls. The live evaluation is a controlled counterfactual protocol: flagged attempts pause before contact and then resume so the would-be outcome can be recorded. Its claim is predictive abstention, not completed autonomous recovery or policy learning. The paper explicitly leaves post-abort completion and longer-horizon monitoring for future work. It therefore supports reporting false aborts, missed failures and subsequent task completion separately.

papers.title: Imitation from Heterogeneous Demonstrations using Grounded Latent-Action World Models
papers.summary: GLAM learns a shared latent-action representation from target robot demonstrations and cheaper auxiliary trajectories that need not carry executable action labels. One model infers latent actions from visual transitions; another uses target action labels to make those latents decodable into robot control. An asymmetric alignment loss transfers the target branch’s control information into the transition-based representation. The resulting model relabels heterogeneous trajectories for a downstream imitation policy. The authors test Kinova robot data and a simulated floating-UMI-gripper source, with an object-mask variant to emphasize manipulated-object motion. They report data-efficiency gains and useful auxiliary-data scaling in these settings. This is evidence for control-grounded representation as an alternative to simply sharing raw action coordinates. It is not demonstrated web-video or human-hand transfer: the source and target share scenes, camera placement, objects and task semantics, and tactile or force information is absent.

papers.title: Memory Anchors for Continual Robot Learning
papers.summary: Memory Anchors studies which old experiences help a robot policy retain earlier tasks during sequential learning. It identifies new-task observations that overlap old-task representations but require different actions, then selects nearby old experiences for replay. For diffusion policies, the project measures action disagreement through conditional denoising to reduce confusion from multiple valid action modes. Controlled experiments remove or enrich these anchors while keeping the replay budget comparable, and the authors report changes in forgetting in simulation and diagnostic real-robot task sequences. The project also emphasizes that replay cannot consist only of high-conflict anchors: diverse old experience remains important. This is persistent policy training from selected past data, not inference-time conversational memory. Extracting anchors needs the model’s representation space and past training data; the evaluated task sequences and robots do not establish unlimited continual deployment.

papers.title: Multisensory Continual Learning: Adapting Pretrained Visuomotor Policies to Force
papers.summary: MuSe asks how a policy pretrained without a sensor can acquire that modality later while preserving its earlier capabilities. The studied case adds force-torque sensing to a pretrained Unified Video-Action model. Early token fusion and later cross-attention adapters combine the sensor with vision and other inputs; the model predicts future observations, force-torque signals and actions. During adaptation, replay mixes the original pretraining data with new multisensory demonstrations, masking the force input and force loss where those measurements are absent. The evaluation separates force prediction on previously unsupervised tasks, forward transfer to new contact-rich tasks and backward transfer to pretraining tasks. The authors report improvements in their tabletop settings, while no-replay ablations exhibit substantial forgetting. This is evidence for a particular sensor-expansion and replay strategy, not a result that every added sensor improves every policy. Only force-torque expansion, limited tasks and access to the original pretraining data were tested; broader modalities, embodiments and longer horizons remain future work.

papers.title: HARBOR: A Harness Framework for Agentic Robot Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: HARBOR automates the engineering workflow surrounding robot reinforcement learning in simulation. A central agent divides a request into bounded stages such as dependencies, task construction, rewards, domain randomization, RL integration and tuning. Stage-local agents operate through standard commands and persistent artifacts. Executable gates check interfaces and rollout evidence before later stages proceed; failures are repaired within a retry budget and unresolved stages can require human intervention. Reward and hyperparameter candidates run in isolated parallel trials, while an experience ledger preserves useful heuristics and failure diagnoses for later runs. This separates the coding agent that constructs or tunes the experiment from the numerical RL algorithm that trains the policy. The authors evaluate multiple simulation backends and include physical validation, but the latter uses user-provided real trajectories, interface engineering and human feedback for simulator alignment. The source explicitly warns that gates do not guarantee semantic policy correctness. Its results support a scoped engineering-automation claim, not a general guarantee that any agent can autonomously train reliable real-world policies.

papers.title: ENPIRE: Agentic Robot Policy Self-Improvement in the Real World
papers.summary: ENPIRE makes selected physical manipulation tasks accessible to coding agents as repeatable research environments. Its Environment component resets scenes and verifies outcomes; Policy Improvement launches a chosen refinement routine; Rollout evaluates candidates on one or more robots; Evolution lets coding agents inspect failures and modify algorithm or infrastructure code. The improvement interface accepts several regimes, including heuristics, code/tool use, behavior cloning, offline RL and online RL. Consequently, the changed artifact can be an executable program, a training recipe or a learned policy, depending on the experiment. The project describes agent-run iterations on prepared tasks such as Push-T and pin insertion, together with simulation experiments and fleet-resource measurements. This is evidence of an engineered loop around real interaction, rather than merely a supervisor choosing skills during one episode. Its autonomy claim is scoped to the provided self-resetting, self-verifying task interfaces. The site labels its showcased 99% result as pass@8, so it should not be rewritten as single-attempt reliability. All results remain author-reported.

papers.title: MobiAgent: Dual-Loop Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
papers.summary: MobiAgent separates deployment-time planning from offline policy refinement. Its inner loop uses a VLM planner, a shared VLM trunk with skill-specific flow-matching action experts, and a reflection critic that recommends advance, retry or replan. Critic observations are retained as episode memory. The outer loop runs after episode termination: it segments and verifies trajectories, standardizes skill captions and trains or fine-tunes neural skill policies. Startup data creates the skill inventory; subsequent rollout data is assigned to the existing inventory, and the described continual phase updates those existing policies without expanding the model inventory. This is more specific than saying the robot simply learns through reasoning or that its skill vocabulary grows without bound. The authors report finite deployment-to-training rounds on RoboCasa and Astribot S1, plus long-horizon BEHAVIOR tasks. Early RoboCasa gains later plateau. Here the reusable changes are learned skill policies and curated data; the paper does not establish indefinite improvement or a learning procedure that recursively redesigns itself.

papers.title: ATOM-Bench: A Real-World Benchmark for Atomic Skills and Compositional Generalization in Manipulation Policies
papers.summary: ATOM-Bench separates learning elementary manipulation skills from recombining them under new task structures. Its motor set isolates physical operations, its instruction set isolates language constraints, and a held-out composition set combines those factors. Models are adapted on atomic tasks only, rather than being shown demonstrations of the compositional test tasks. The project describes paired single-arm Franka Panda and dual-arm Cobot Magic tracks, with fixed physical test seeds and metrics for task completion, partial progress and composition failures. The reported models often perform much better on atomic tasks than on held-out combinations. This is useful evidence for asking what a benchmark score actually measures: a successful familiar operation is not automatically evidence of compositional reuse. The scope remains tabletop manipulation on these platforms and these adaptation protocols, not general home or factory performance. The project page reports results for its selected policies; it does not establish that every VLA has the same failure profile.

papers.title: H2RBench: A Real-to-Sim Benchmark for Evaluating Human-to-Robot Transfer
papers.summary: H2RBench compares human-to-robot transfer methods under a shared task and supervision protocol. It reconstructs real workspaces in simulation, uses real human demonstrations, and holds the robot-demonstration budget fixed while varying the amount of human data. The evaluated methods bridge embodiments through visual editing, keypoints, latent dynamics or hierarchical subgoals. The reported human-data benefit varies by method and task: it is more consistent for coarse spatial behavior than for precise contact and longer sequences, and adding human data can hurt insertion performance. The benchmark also compares rankings from separately trained simulation-pipeline and real-world-pipeline policies. That correspondence supports comparative evaluation in the tested setup; it does not show that a single simulated policy transfers unchanged to arbitrary real settings. The task suite remains limited to controlled third-person tabletop manipulation, primarily with rigid objects.
